title: 35 meters needed, 36 bought: why there are not enough stock lengths for ten parts
description: Ten whole parts of 3.5 m cannot be obtained from six 6 m stock lengths. We check cutting, discreteness of blanks and the error of dividing total footage.
seo_title: 35 meters needed, 36 bought: why there are not enough stock lengths for ten parts
seo_description: Ten whole parts of 3.5 m cannot be obtained from six 6 m stock lengths. We check cutting, discreteness of blanks and the error of dividing total footage.
seo_keywords: cutting calculation, stock length procurement, whole blank, material footage
content:
For ten parts of 3.5 meters, procurement calculated the total length of 35 meters and ordered six six-meter stock lengths. There will be 36 meters in stock — formally more than the need. But ten whole parts cannot be obtained from them: only one such blank fits into each stock length. The error lies in the transition from total footage to the number of discrete source elements.

Why a one-meter reserve saves nothing

Consider a conditional bill of quantities: ten whole elements of exactly 3.5 m are needed. Only source stock lengths of 6 m are allowed, joints to obtain one part are prohibited by the task. For clarity, we initially neglect saw kerf width and end losses. Tolerances, material and other characteristics are confirmed and are not the subject of this check.

The total required footage is indeed 10 × 3.5 = 35 m. Division 35 / 6 gives approximately 5.83. Rounding up to six establishes only a lower estimate of the number of stock lengths by total resource. It does not yet show whether the required whole parts can be placed in these stock lengths.

Two blanks would require 3.5 + 3.5 = 7 m, which is more than the available 6 m. Therefore each source stock length yields at most one required part. Six stock lengths give six parts, not ten. The shortage is four whole elements, although the total footage received exceeds the length of the finished set.

Proof of the required number of stock lengths

Since two blanks cannot be obtained from one stock length, at least ten stock lengths are needed for ten blanks. Ten is also sufficient in our idealized model: one part of 3.5 m is taken from each. The lower bound is achieved by a specific scheme, therefore the minimum for the given conditions is ten.

The total source length will be 60 m, the finished elements will occupy 35 m, the remainders 25 m. This is not an arithmetic error and not an automatically inflated request. Each of the ten stock lengths will have 2.5 m left. It is precisely the distribution of the remainder across separate source units that does not allow turning it into additional whole parts 3.5 m long.

With a positive saw kerf width, the available remainder becomes smaller. But this does not explain the initial shortage: six stock lengths are unsuitable even with zero losses. For a real technological task, the kerf, allowances and usable length are additionally checked. Here ten is a proven solution only in the explicitly given model, not a ready production norm.

Can two remainders be combined?

Two remainders of 2.5 m total 5 m of material. However, a whole part of 3.5 m can be obtained from them only with a change of the initial condition prohibiting a joint. Proposing to weld or otherwise join the cut-offs already refers to a different technical solution. The procurement specialist cannot silently allow it for the footage to match.

Remainders may have value for other parts, if those are provided and the material suits. Then they are accounted in the corresponding cutting task, not declared universally useless waste. But the future possibility of use does not close the current need for ten whole elements. For it, the initial supply still has only six suitable blanks.

Which table really checks procurement

A scheme of placing parts in each source stock length is needed. For our case it is very simple: stock lengths 1–10, one part of 3.5 m and a calculated remainder of 2.5 m in each, before accounting for technological losses. In the erroneous variant, six rows cannot be distributed over ten required parts without exceeding the length of at least one stock length.

In a more complex set, short parts can be placed next to long ones. Then the quantity depends on permissible combinations. Checking only the sum of lengths does not see these constraints. A similar mathematical distinction is presented in the bin packing model in Google OR-Tools documentation: each item is assigned to one source capacity, and each capacity is checked separately.

For our simple bill of quantities, a software optimizer is not required. It is enough that 7 > 6 and that each of the ten parts must be obtained whole from one stock length. A complex program with an incorrectly allowed part split could also produce an attractive but unusable result.

What to write in the remark to the application

State the specific reason: "Six stock lengths of 6 m provide total footage, but yield at most six whole parts of 3.5 m. Ten parts without joints are required. In the adopted model, ten source stock lengths are needed." Thus the correction relates to the number of procurement units, not to the length of already agreed elements.

If footage in the bill of quantities does not turn into a feasible supply, send a request to institute "Nedra" for checking the requirement calculation. Attach the part lengths, available source sizes and joint restrictions. These data allow checking physical feasibility of the application before ordering material.
